about.title: Special Products: Three Shortcuts for Multiplying
about.length_note: About 30 minutes fits. There are three patterns, each taught alone with an example and a check. The long-way warm-up and the number tricks at the end fill the rest. A learner who wants more time can pause after any check question.

say.text: Welcome to class 35. Last time you multiplied polynomials the long way. Today you learn three shortcuts that save a lot of time.
First, a word we need. A binomial is an expression with exactly two terms, like x + 3. To square it, we multiply it by itself.

ask.why: The little 2 applies to the whole binomial. It means the binomial times itself, so (x + 3)² is (x + 3)(x + 3). It is not x² + 9.

say.text: Let's do (x + 3)(x + 3) the long way. Multiply every term by every term. That gives four small products.
Now add them up: x² + 3x + 3x + 9. The two middle terms are twins, so they combine. We get x² + 6x + 9.

ask.q: Using the long way, what is (x + 2)(x + 2)?
ask.why: Multiply every term by every term: x², 2x, 2x and 4. The two middle terms combine to 4x. That gives x² + 4x + 4.

say.text: Here is the shortcut. To square a sum, square the first term, square the last term, and double their product for the middle.
Try it on (x + 3)². First term squared: x². Middle: 2 · x · 3 = 6x. Last term squared: 9. That is x² + 6x + 9, the same as the long way.

show.text:
first²: x²
double the product: 2 · x · 3 = 6x
last²: 3² = 9

say.text: Your turn. Use the shortcut: square the first, double the product, square the last.

ask.why: First squared is x². Double the product is 2 · x · 5 = 10x. Last squared is 25. Leaving out the middle term, as in x² + 25, is the most common slip.

say.text: Why is there a middle term? Picture a square with sides of length a + b. Cut it into a small a-by-a square, a small b-by-b square, and two a-by-b rectangles. The two rectangles make the 2ab.

show.text: A big square with side a + b, split into four pieces. Top-left is a square a by a. Bottom-right is a square b by b. The other two corners are matching rectangles a by b.

say.text: Test it with plain numbers. 25² is (20 + 5)². That is 400 + 200 + 25, which is 625. And 25 times 25 really is 625. Because it works for every number, it is called an identity.

ask.right: No. It is missing the middle term 6x.
wrong: Yes, because squaring spreads over each term
Yes, but only when x is positive
ask.why: Try x = 1. (1 + 3)² is 16, but 1² + 9 is only 10. The real answer is x² + 6x + 9, and it needs the middle term.

say.text: Now a minus sign. (a − b)² follows the same pattern. Only the middle sign flips.

Example: (x − 4)². First squared: x². Middle: 2 · x · (−4) = −8x. Last squared: (−4)² = +16. So it is x² − 8x + 16. Notice the last term stays positive, because a negative times a negative is positive.

show.text:
first²: x²
double the product: 2 · x · (−4) = −8x
last²: (−4)² = 16

say.text: Your turn with a minus sign. Remember the middle flips and the last stays positive.

ask.why: First squared is y². Double the product is 2 · y · (−6) = −12y. Last squared is (−6)² = +36. The middle is negative, but the last term is positive.

say.text: The first and last terms can have numbers in front. Square the whole term. In (2x + 5)², the first term is 2x, and (2x)² = 4x². The middle is 2 · 2x · 5 = 20x. The last is 25.

ask.why: (3x)² = 9x², because the 3 gets squared too. The middle is 2 · 3x · 1 = 6x. The last is 1² = 1.

say.text: Here is a game example. A square map has sides of x + 2 tiles. Its area is (x + 2)², which is x² + 4x + 4. If x is 10, the map is 12 by 12, so 144 tiles. And 100 + 40 + 4 is also 144.

show.text: A square game map with each side labelled x + 2 tiles.

say.text: Now the second shortcut. Conjugates are two binomials with the same terms, but one has a plus and the other a minus. Like (x + 5) and (x − 5).
Multiply (x + 5)(x − 5) the long way: x² − 5x + 5x − 25. The middle terms cancel to zero. We are left with x² − 25, only two terms.

show.text:
x · x = x²
x · (−5) = −5x
5 · x = +5x
5 · (−5) = −25
middle terms add to 0, so x² − 25

say.text: That is the pattern. For a sum times a difference, square the first term, square the last term, and subtract. The result is called a difference of squares.
Example: (2x + 5)(2x − 5). Square the first: (2x)² = 4x². Square the last: 25. Subtract: 4x² − 25. There is no middle term.

ask.why: Square the first to get x². Square the last to get 64. Subtract them to get x² − 64. The sign between the two terms is minus, because the middle terms cancel.

say.text: Now we have two patterns, so spotting which one you have matters. A binomial squared gives three terms. A sum times a difference gives only two.

show.text: Binomial square: (a + b)² or (a − b)², three terms | Sum and difference: (a + b)(a − b), two terms

ask.q: Which of these multiplies out to only two terms?
ask.why: Only a sum times a difference of the same two terms has middle terms that cancel. That gives x² − 49. The others each have a middle term and give three terms.

say.text: Here is a fun use. 97 × 103 is (100 − 3)(100 + 3). That is 100² − 3², or 10,000 − 9. The answer is 9,991, with no calculator.

ask.why: Square the first: 50² = 2,500. Square the last: 1² = 1. Subtract to get 2,499. Adding instead would give 2,501, which is the wrong sign.

say.text: Let's gather the three patterns. Square the first, square the last, and then decide what goes in the middle. Great work today.

show.text:
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²

say.text: Next class we run these patterns backwards to factor. A difference of squares turns back into a sum-and-difference pair. Rest well, and see you in class 36.

show.text: Next: read the patterns in reverse to factor

other_side.claim: Learn the three special-product patterns as quick shortcuts.
other_side.other_view: Patterns are fast once you spot them, and OpenStax teaches them for that reason. But the long method of multiplying every term by every term always works. Paul Dawkins, a university math instructor, warns that memorizing a formula without understanding how to use it will not carry a student through a math class. Many teachers therefore pair the patterns with the area picture and a number check, as this lesson does.
